pr_title: perf: Combine small chunks in sinks for streaming pipelines
pr_body:
Fixes #11699 

Small chunks add significant overhead. This PR merges them in the sink. If there are lots of small chunks, this should make things faster. If there are lots of large chunks, it adds a little overhead but it's fixed and small per chunk, so that's fine. There may however be a slow down in some midway edge cases where the chunk merging involves copying extra data.

This doesn't fix the fact that small chunks are being generated, though... I will file a separate PR for the specific edge case in the reproducer script, and file an issue for another likely case if I can reproduce it.

### Benchmark

Before:

```
$ python ../11699.py 
SINK 2.8767316341400146
COLLECT+WRITE 0.9260973930358887
STREAMING COLLECT+WRITE 4.061856031417847
```

After:

```
$ python ../11699.py
SINK 1.064814805984497
COLLECT+WRITE 0.9025135040283203
STREAMING COLLECT+WRITE 1.1788344383239746
```

Using this script:

```python
from datetime import datetime

import polars as pl

start_datetime = datetime(2020, 1, 1)
end_datetime = datetime(
    2024,
    1,
    1,
)
N_ids = 10
interval = "1m"
df = (
    pl.LazyFrame(
        {
            "time": pl.datetime_range(
                start_datetime, end_datetime, interval=interval, eager=True
            )
        }
    )
    .join(
        pl.LazyFrame(
            {"id": [f"id{i:05d}" for i in range(N_ids)], "value": list(range(N_ids))}
        ),
        how="cross",
    )
    .select("time", "id", "value")
)

# print(df.profile(streaming=True))
from time import time

start = time()
df.sink_parquet("/tmp/out.parquet")
print("SINK", time() - start)

start = time()
df.collect().write_parquet("/tmp/out2.parquet")
print("COLLECT+WRITE", time() - start)

start = time()
df.collect(streaming=True).write_parquet("/tmp/out3.parquet")
print("STREAMING COLLECT+WRITE", time() - start)
```

issue_context.title: `sink_parquet(...)` much slower than `.collect().write_parquet(...)`
issue_context.body:
### Checks

- [X] I have checked that this issue has not already been reported.

- [X] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [latest version](https://pypi.org/project/polars/) of Polars.


### Reproducible example

Using the same data as in https://github.com/pola-rs/polars/issues/11698, I'm observing at least a 2x performance difference in the following:

```python
pl.scan_parquet(f).sink_parquet("/tmp/out")

# 2x faster:
pl.scan_parquet(f).collect().write_parquet("/tmp/out")
```


Interestingly when looking at htop, the version with `.collect()` seems to use all cores sometimes (during reading?) while the other version never uses more than ~ 1 core.

This is a reduced example; the original tables has many more columns and the performance difference is much larger.

### Log output

_No response_

### Issue description

See example

### Expected behavior

Should have similar performance.

review_comments: Very crude solution. Can you test how this will perform with a single threaded `rechunk`?

The issue is that if you just do a rechunk of `chunks`, you're limited to merging by the number of cores. E.g. with 12 cores, you merge 12 chunks, and that's all you merge. If you have 2 cores, you only merge 2 chunks, so the performance ends up being much worse if you have a stream of many small chunks. I can do another round of benchmarks tomorrow demonstrating that, but that's my memory from previous testing that led me to this strategy.
Notice that `chunks` size is `morsels_per_sink` which is the size of the thread pool, basically. So the fewer cores you have, the less merging only `chunks` helps.

> f you have 2 cores, you only merge 2 chunks, so the performance ends up being much worse if you have a stream of many small chunks. I can do another round of benchmarks tomorrow demonstrating that, but that's my memory from previous testing that led me to this strategy.

I don't really follow, because a `vstack_mut` is essentially the same. It only has one downside that is that we cannot know the size to allocate. So we can trigger multiple reallocations. With a `rechunk` we first do a pass to determine the required output memory size and then we trigger the memcopies. That's the reason I think we should just `rechunk`.

So I took this as an opportunity to learn Divan, it's pretty cool: https://github.com/itamarst/benchmarks/blob/main/polars-vstack/benches/vstack.rs#L13

Running this I get:


I'm really not getting the impression that repeated `vstack_mut` leads to quadratic slowdown. Runtime is linear, allocated memory is linear and much smaller than underlying data: 100_000 * 1000 * 8 bytes is 800MB, but only 12MB gets allocated.

Next going to read the code for `vstack_mut` so I understand implementation better.
So AFAICT `vstack_mut` eventually devolves to `new_chunks()` in `chunked_array/ops/append.rs`, which clones all the chunks individually, i.e. does not make them contiguous.

> I'm really not getting the impression that repeated vstack_mut leads to quadratic slowdown

No, I don't mean quadratic slowdown. It is a quadratic growing strategy. Which means we might have a few reallocs.

Alright. What I mean is that we need a combination of the strategies. So:

1. Batch chunks across multiple batches. Agree on that
2. Combine them into a single chunk. Also agree on that, but I think we should use `rechunk` (all batches just before flush) instead of `vstack_mut` here.

Maybe I'm missing something in the API search, but `rechunk()` seems to be specific to a single `Series`/`DataFrame`? Which would help if the series of incoming `Series` were:

```
Series<[2.5K chunk, 2.5K chunk, 2.5K chunk, 2.5K chunk, 2.5K chunk, 2.5K chunk]>
Series<[2.5K chunk, 2.5K chunk, 2.5K chunk, 2.5K chunk, 2.5K chunk, 2.5K chunk]>
Series<[2.5K chunk, 2.5K chunk, 2.5K chunk, 2.5K chunk, 2.5K chunk, 2.5K chunk]>
...
```

But actually what is being processed is:

```
Series<[2.5K chunk]>
Series<[2.5K chunk]>
Series<[2.5K chunk]>
Series<[2.5K chunk]>
...
```

So `rechunk()` on an individual `Series` won't help, you need to combine them somehow, and `vstack_mut` (or perhaps the lower cost `vstack_mut_unchecked`, if it were public) seems to be the only option.

Yes. you first combine them into a single `DataFrame` with multiple chunks and then you `rechunk`. Depening on the sink this should be done parallel (`as_single_chunk_par`) or single threaded `as_single_chunk`. Here we should do it single threaded.

So I agree with most of the code here, I just want to use `rechunk` as it allocates properly. If you want I can finish the PR (I expect it to be minor changes).

Re-reading all this again, my impression is that you want the _caller_ to decide whether and how to rechunk, instead of, as is currently implemented, `SemicontiguousVstacker` having a fixed policy of calling `as_single_chunk()`.

I tested the code with `as_single_chunk_par`. It appeared to cause a deadlock in the `sink_parquet()` case :grimacing: which I didn't investigate further. It did indeed make the `collect(streaming=True).write_parquet()` version slightly faster.

So I will try implement the above, and if it's still not you meant please do finish the PR, yes.
